senses.gloss:
Kṣīrabhavānī
(‘Bhavānī [the Divine मोथेर्] [who is fond of] milk’)
------------------------------------------
Kāśmīra or the modern Kashmir is one of the very old parts of India full of several sacred spots. An ancient and voluminous work called the Bhṛṅgīśa Saṁhitā, fragments of which only are available now, that too in the manuscript form, is said to contain details of all these places.
Kṣīrabhavānī TempleAlong with the Amaranāth cave and the Vaiṣṇo देवी shrine, क्षीरभवानी ranks as the third centre of Hindu पिल्ग्रिमगे in Kashmir.
According to one version, it is one of the 51 शक्तिपीठस् where the neck of the सती दाक्षायणी fell. (See TANTRAS.)
The Kṣīrabhavāṇi (or the modern Khir Bhawani) is situated at the village Tulāmūla (or Tulamulla), which is 4 kms. (2.5 miles) from Gandharbal and 44 kms. (27 miles) to the north west of the capital Srinagar. The temple is a small structure of marble with its dome covered by thin gold leaf. The present temple was built by the Mahārāja Pratāp Siṅgh in A. D. 1912. It contains the images of the देवी known as Mahārājñā and of शिव called Trisandheśvara. It is situated inside a kuṇḍa, a natural water tank of small size, hexagonal in shape. The water constantly supplied by several natural springs is about 2 metres (6.5 ft.) deep.
This water is often changing its colour, the colours usually seen being white, red, brown, yellow, blue and black. People believe that when the water turns blackish, it is a bad omen for the country.
All worship by the devotees is offered to the waters of the kuṇḍa from outside. Kṣīra (milk) and miṣṭānna (rice pudding) are considered dear to the goddess.
Jyeṣṭha-śukla-aṣṭamī (generally occurring during June) is the main festival day when pilgrims throng in thousands.
The shrine complex is being taken care of by the Dharmarth Trust of the State. It has effected several improvements as follows: a pūjāmaṇṭapa measuring 10 by 5 metres (34 ft. by 17 ft.) in front of the kuṇḍa; sheds for performing homas (fire-rituals); an electric pump to clean the water of the kuṇḍa, generally once in 2 to 3 years; Dharmaśālas or guest-houses for the visiting pilgrims.
The little island containing the kuṇḍa of the देवी is full of Chinar trees.
Each one of the ब्राह्मण families in Kashmir has a kuladevatā (goddess of the family). Kṣīrabhavāṇi is the goddess for most of them.
A brief account of the local legends may be given here:
The देवी (Kālī or पार्वती) got angry with the demon king रावण, in whose kingdom she had settled, and asked हनुमान् along with 360 नागस् (snake-chieftains) to take her to Kāśmīra. हनुमान् did so, settling the देवी in her different aspects, in different places. The नागस् too were given appropriate places to live.
According to another version, the देवी shifted to Kāśmīra from लङ्का and started begging for ड़ोओद् from the houses of a few ब्राह्मणस्. They gave her kṣīra or inspissated milk. She settled down at the present place of पिल्ग्रिमगे. Later on, a temple was built there.
As regards the discovery of this place also, there are two stories. According to the first, the goddess appeared to one Pandit Govind Joo Gadru and showed him the place. When he saw it, he poured milk which he had brought in a number of earthern vessels into the spring.
According to the second, a pious ब्राह्मण, Kṛṣṇapaṇḍita by name, was informed by a divine being about the existence of the spring of the Divine मोथेर्. As directed by the being, the Paṇḍit started in a boat and went behind a serpent that guided him to the marshy spot. The paṇḍit then got it filled up with several loads of earth to prepare the present place of पिल्ग्रिमगे.

Kṣīrasvāmin
------------------------------------------
Of all the lexicons in Sanskrit, the Amarakoṣa of अमरसिṁह (5th century A. D.) is the most famous one and has attracted many scholars to comment and expound it. One of the better known commentators is Kṣīra or क्षीरस्वामिन् who was a scholar attached to the court of the king Jayaprada of Kashmir and might have lived in the 8th century A. D. Other sources assign him to the 11th century A. D. His commentary is known as Amarakoṣodghāṭana.
Kṣīrasvāmin is said to have composed a commentary on the Dhātupāṭha of पाणिनि (5th century B. C.) also.

kṣipta
(‘thrown about’)
------------------------------------------
According to the Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) the चित्त or the मिन्द् has five states. क्षिप्त is the first state. In this state the मिन्द् is constantly thrown about (kṣip = to throw) from one sense-object to another. Hence no योग or concentration is possible in this state.

kṣīrasamudra
(‘ocean of milk’)
------------------------------------------
The पुराणस् describe seven oceans (sapta-mahāsamudras) in the universe. Out of them, the क्षीरसमुद्र (the ocean of milk) also is one. It surrounds the island called Krauñcadvīpa.
It is said to have been formed by the profuse outflow of milk from the udder of the celestial cow सुरभि.
Mahāviṣṇu is said to have made it his abode, wherein he lies on the serpent शेष which is floating on the ocean.
It is by churning this ocean that अमृत or ambrosia was produced. (See SAMUDRA-MATHANA.)
According to another version, शिव is said to have given this ocean of milk to उपमन्यु, the young son of the sage Vyāghrapāda.
